messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 46
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Auditor
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 41

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Feeling Happy: Feeling happy or relaxed, Spatial Triggers: Physical locations, Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark
  Maladaptive Strategies: Smoking: I smoke, Avoid Relaxation: avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous, Avoid Talking: Talking with others about the event or its aftermath
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
  Negative Appraisals: Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Kavi

Kavi was forty-two when the cyclone hit Fiji. He had been living in Suva for fifteen years, working as an auditor for a shipping firm, and had built a life that felt, finally, stable—a wife, a modest house on the outskirts of the city, colleagues who knew his name. When the storm warnings came, he and his wife Priya had done what they always did: secured the shutters, gathered supplies, and settled in to wait. The radio crackled with updates. The wind came first as a distant roar, then as something that seemed to shake the very foundation of the house. Around midnight, the roof began to fail. Kavi remembered the sound most vividly—a tearing, a collapse—and then the rain came in sheets, cold and relentless. He remembered reaching for Priya in the dark, his hand finding only water. The next morning, when the wind finally stopped, she was gone. They found her three days later, two blocks away, caught against a fence. 

Four years had passed since then, and Kavi had learned to survive in a body that no longer felt entirely his own. He had moved to the United States on a work visa, taken a position as an auditor in Portland, and established a routine so carefully constructed that it resembled a life. But the world had become a place where danger lived in the gaps he could not see. He was certain now that bad things were not random—they were waiting, patient, for him to relax his vigilance. When moments of peace or contentment would arrive unbidden—a quiet afternoon, a colleague's laugh that made him smile—Kavi would feel a sharp jolt of fear. These pockets of happiness triggered an immediate spike in his threat detection. He had come to believe that relaxation was itself a warning sign, a moment when his defenses were down and something catastrophic was about to occur. The feeling of being at ease made him reach for a cigarette, made him scan his surroundings for danger, made his mind suddenly flood with sensory fragments from that night—the metallic taste of blood in his mouth, the smell of wet concrete and something else, something like rust or rot, that he could not name.

The triggers compounded. At night, when darkness fell and he lay in bed, his mind would spiral into threat assessment. He would check his phone obsessively, looking for alerts, news of storms, anything that might explain the dread that seized him. Silence in particular had become intolerable. If his apartment was quiet—no traffic, no voices from neighboring units—he felt certain that something terrible was imminent, that the world was holding its breath before it broke. When a work project ran late, when a meeting took longer than expected, Kavi's mind immediately constructed a narrative of disaster. He avoided unfamiliar places entirely, convinced that he could not possibly assess the danger lurking in spaces he did not know. This meant declining invitations to new restaurants, avoiding neighborhoods outside his carefully mapped routes, and, increasingly, finding reasons not to leave his apartment on weekends.

The memories themselves had become unbearable in their vividness. When they surfaced—and they surfaced constantly—they came complete with sensation. He would taste copper and ash. His nose would fill with the smell of rain-soaked earth and something acrid that he associated with the moment before the roof collapsed. The memory felt so extreme, so overwhelming in its sensory detail, that part of him had begun to doubt whether it had truly happened the way his body insisted it had. This dissociation offered a strange kind of relief, even as it terrified him. If it was not real, then he had not truly lost her. But he knew, in the rational part of his mind that still functioned, that it was real, and that his disbelief was itself a symptom of how broken he had become.

The smoking had increased steadily. What had begun as an occasional stress response had become a constant companion—a cigarette first thing in the morning, another before work, several during the day, a chain of them in the evening as darkness fell. The ritual gave him something to do with his hands, a way to manage the feeling that he could not stop bad things from happening, that the world was fundamentally dangerous and he was fundamentally powerless within it. But the smoking also trapped him in a cycle. Each cigarette was a small reinforcement that the danger was real, that he was right to be afraid, that his hypervigilance was justified. And the more he smoked, the more he felt the weight of his own deadness—a numbness that had settled into his chest and seemed to have calcified there, making it impossible to feel anything but dread and the faint, mechanical satisfaction of nicotine.

He had stopped talking to anyone about what had happened. His sister called from Auckland every few weeks, and he would tell her he was fine, that work was fine, that he was adjusting. The lie was easier than the truth, and the truth felt dangerous anyway—as though speaking it aloud would give it more power, would make it more real. His colleagues at the firm had learned not to ask. He kept his desk organized, his reports meticulous, his interactions brief and professional. What frightened him most now was not the memory itself but the possibility that he would relax, that he would allow himself to feel something other than vigilance, and that in that moment of weakness the next disaster would strike. He had begun to understand his own survival as a kind of debt—he had lived while Priya had not, and that imbalance could not stand. The world would collect. He was certain of it. Three weeks ago, after a particularly bad night where he had not slept at all, convinced that the silence in his apartment meant something was wrong, Kavi had finally called a therapist. He did not know what help looked like anymore, but he knew he could not continue like this. What he wanted most was to feel something other than fear. What he was most afraid of was that even if he did, it would kill him.
